p.src: Supersymmetry is among the most abstract constructions in physics. It resembles rotations and translations because it is a symmetry, but it does not fit inside ordinary spacetime without enlarging what we mean by a coordinate. Its natural parameters are Grassmann quantities: objects that can be added and multiplied, yet anticommute rather than commute.

p.src: Odd and even elements

u.src: Odd and even elements
en: Odd and even elements

p.src:
Let $\epsilon_i$ denote independent Grassmann generators. They obey $\epsilon_i\epsilon_j=-\epsilon_j\epsilon_i,
\qquad
\{\epsilon_i,\epsilon_j\}=0.$ Setting $i=j$ gives $2\epsilon_i^2=0,
\qquad
\epsilon_i^2=0,$ over the real or complex numbers. The generator is not zero; only its square is zero.

p.src:
Each homogeneous element has a parity. A product containing an odd number of Grassmann generators is odd, while a product containing an even number is even: $\begin{aligned}
\text{odd}\times\text{odd}&=\text{even},\\
\text{odd}\times\text{even}&=\text{odd},\\
\text{even}\times\text{even}&=\text{even}.\end{aligned}$ Even elements commute with homogeneous elements. Two odd elements anticommute. Thus $n\epsilon_i=\epsilon_i n,
\qquad
\epsilon_i\epsilon_j=-\epsilon_j\epsilon_i,$ when $n$ is even.

p.src:
A function of one Grassmann variable has only two possible powers: $f(\epsilon)=a+b\epsilon.$ There is no $\epsilon^2$ term. With two independent generators, $f(\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)
=a+b_1\epsilon_1+b_2\epsilon_2+c\epsilon_1\epsilon_2.$ The expansion stops after both generators have appeared. For $n$ independent generators, the ordered monomials form a $2^n$-dimensional basis: $1,\quad
\epsilon_i,\quad
\epsilon_i\epsilon_j,\quad
\ldots,\quad
\epsilon_1\epsilon_2\cdots\epsilon_n.$

p.src:
When two real generators are combined into a complex pair $\theta,\bar\theta$, a general function can be written, with a chosen ordering, as $f(\theta,\bar\theta)
=a+\bar b\,\theta+\bar\theta\,b+c\,\bar\theta\theta.$ The bar indicates the complex-pair notation used here. Reversing the final order changes a sign: $\bar\theta\theta=-\theta\bar\theta.$

p.src: It is usually convenient to assign the whole function a definite parity. If $f$ is even, then $a$ and $c$ are even while $b$ and $\bar b$ are odd. If $f$ is odd, those assignments reverse. The coefficients may themselves belong to a larger Grassmann algebra, provided they do not depend on the particular variables with respect to which we are expanding.

p.src:
We use a left Grassmann derivative. Its defining local rules are $\partial_\theta a=0,
\qquad
\partial_\theta(\theta B)=B,$ when $a$ and $B$ are independent of $\theta$. Before differentiating, move the relevant $\theta$ to the left. Every passage through another odd factor changes the sign.

p.src:
Return to $f(\theta,\bar\theta)
=a+\bar b\,\theta+\bar\theta\,b+c\,\bar\theta\theta.$ Suppose first that $f$ is even. Then $\bar b$ is odd and $c$ is even. Reordering the terms that contain $\theta$, $\begin{aligned}
\bar b\,\theta&=-\theta\bar b,\\
c\,\bar\theta\theta&=-\theta c\,\bar\theta.\end{aligned}$ Therefore $\partial_\theta f=-\bar b-c\bar\theta.$

p.src: Coordinate and derivative as operators

u.src: Coordinate and derivative as operators
en: Coordinate and derivative as operators

p.src:
The Grassmann analogue uses an anticommutator. Take $f(\theta)=a+\theta b,$ with $a$ even and $b$ odd, so that $f$ is even. First, $\theta\partial_\theta f=\theta b.$ In the opposite order, $\begin{aligned}
\partial_\theta(\theta f)
&=\partial_\theta(\theta a+\theta^2b)\\
&=a.\end{aligned}$ Adding the two orders gives the original function: $\left(\partial_\theta\theta+\theta\partial_\theta\right)f
=a+\theta b=f.$ Hence $\boxed{\{\partial_\theta,\theta\}=1.}$ The derivative $\partial_\theta$ is itself odd. That is why its canonical relation with the odd coordinate is an anticommutator.

p.src: Integration

u.src: Integration
en: Integration

p.src:
The integral over one Grassmann variable is fixed by $\int d\theta\,1=0,
\qquad
\int d\theta\,\theta=1.$ Consequently, for $f(\theta)=a+\theta b$, $\int d\theta\,f(\theta)=b=\partial_\theta f(\theta).$ Thus integration and differentiation perform the same component extraction. This is the Berezin integral. Its normalization is the unique simple choice compatible with translation invariance and Grassmann integration by parts.

p.src: Consider a continuous unitary group with Hermitian generators $G_i$. Near the identity, $U(\alpha)=\mathbf 1+i\alpha^iG_i+O(\alpha^2),$ where the $\alpha^i$ are ordinary commuting parameters. The infinitesimal multiplication law is encoded by the Lie algebra $=i f_{ij}{}^{k}G_k.$ The constants $f_{ij}{}^k$ are the structure constants. Closure means that commuting any two generators returns a linear combination of generators already in the algebra.

p.src:
For a single fermionic mode, introduce $c_+$ and $c_-$: $\{c_-,c_+\}=1,
\qquad
\{c_+,c_+\}=\{c_-,c_-\}=0.$ Therefore $c_+^2=c_-^2=0,
\qquad
N_F=c_+c_-,$ and the occupation number is only $0$ or $1$. The bosonic operators are even, the fermionic operators are odd, and every $a_\pm$ commutes with every $c_\pm$.

p.src:
Assume the boson and fermion have the same rest energy $m$, and define $Q=\sqrt m\,a_+c_-,
\qquad
\bar Q=Q^\dagger=\sqrt m\,a_-c_+.$ The operator $Q$ removes one fermion and creates one boson. Its conjugate removes one boson and creates one fermion. Each contains one fermionic operator and is therefore odd.

\{\bar Q,\bar Q\}=2\bar Q^2=0,$ because $Q^2$ contains $c_-^2$ and $\bar Q^2$ contains $c_+^2$.

p.src:
What remains is the relation with $H$. Let $H\ket{E}=E\ket{E}.$ If the boson and fermion masses are equal, $Q$ replaces one by the other without changing the energy. Hence $Q\ket{E}$ is either zero or another eigenstate with the same eigenvalue: $H Q\ket{E}=E Q\ket{E}.$ On the other hand, $QH\ket{E}=Q(E\ket{E})=E Q\ket{E}.$ Subtracting, $\ket{E}=0.$ If the energy eigenstates form a complete basis, this holds as an operator identity: $=0,
\qquad
[H,\bar Q]=0.$

p.src:
The complete toy algebra is therefore $\begin{aligned}
\{Q,\bar Q\}&=H,\\
\{Q,Q\}&=\{\bar Q,\bar Q\}=0,\\
[H,Q]&=[H,\bar Q]=0.\end{aligned}$ The supercharges are conserved odd charges. More surprisingly, their algebra mixes an operation that changes particle type with the generator of spacetime translation.

p.src: Now invent a transformation that shifts an odd coordinate: $\theta\longmapsto\theta+\epsilon,$ where $\epsilon$ is another odd Grassmann parameter. At the same time, let time acquire an even nilpotent displacement, $t\longmapsto t+i\bar\theta\epsilon.$ Both $\bar\theta$ and $\epsilon$ are odd, so their product is even and can consistently be added to the even coordinate $t$.

u.src: The geometric meaning
en: The geometric meaning

p.src:
The algebra now has two equivalent realizations. In the oscillator picture, $Q$ and $\bar Q$ replace fermions by bosons and bosons by fermions. In the geometric picture, $q$ and $\bar q$ translate a function through odd directions while inducing an ordinary time shift. In both pictures, $\begin{gathered}
\{\text{supercharge},\text{conjugate supercharge}\}\\
=\text{time-translation generator}.
\end{gathered}$

p.src: The generalized coordinate space containing $t,\theta,\bar\theta$ is superspace. In a relativistic field theory it also contains the ordinary spatial coordinates, and the supercharges close on the full spacetime momentum $P_\mu$, not only on $H=P_0$. Curving this structure leads toward supergravity.

p.src: In one sense Grassmann variables are an efficient bookkeeping device for bosons and fermions. In another, the closure relation says something much deeper: the distinction between particle type and spacetime geometry is no longer absolute. Moving twice in odd directions produces motion in an ordinary direction. Whether nature realizes that structure experimentally is separate from the mathematical fact that the structure is coherent, economical, and remarkably rigid.
